units.t: Space Exploration. Episode one.
In this episode: How rockets work, The Space Race, Apollo and the Moon landing and Australia's place in space.
Part one. How rockets work.
A rocket doesn't push against the air.
It throws mass out the back so fast that the rest of it has no choice but to go forward.
Action and reaction.
Every rocket relies on Newton's third law: for every action there is an equal and opposite reaction.
Burning propellant makes hot gas at enormous pressure, and the nozzle forces it out the back at several kilometres per second.
Pushing that mass backwards pushes the rocket forwards.
A garden hose kicks in your hand, and a balloon zips around the room, for the same reason.
A common myth is that rockets push against the air, so they couldn't work in space.
They work slightly better in a vacuum, because no air pressure resists the exhaust.
What they do need is oxygen to burn their fuel, so they carry their own oxidiser.
Common pairings are refined kerosene with liquid oxygen, and liquid hydrogen with liquid oxygen.
Solid boosters mix fuel and oxidiser into a rubbery solid.
Mostly fuel, built in stages.
Getting to space is so demanding that a rocket is mostly a flying fuel tank.
Typically 85 to 90% of a large rocket's lift-off mass is propellant, and the payload is often only a few per cent.
A Falcon 9 weighs about 550 tonnes at lift-off but carries at most around 23 tonnes to low orbit, roughly 4%.
Every extra kilogram of fuel also has to be lifted, which needs yet more fuel.
Carrying empty tanks wastes energy, so most rockets are built in stages.
The large first stage does the heavy lifting through the thick lower atmosphere, then shuts down and falls away.
A smaller second stage pushes a much lighter vehicle onwards, and some rockets add a third.
Staging is the practical answer to the harsh arithmetic of the rocket equation.
Orbit is about speed.
Reaching space is surprisingly easy: the commonly used boundary, the Kármán line, is only about 100 kilometres up.
Staying there is the hard part.
An object in orbit is constantly falling towards Earth, but moving sideways so fast that the ground curves away beneath it.
In low Earth orbit that takes about 7.
8 kilometres per second, roughly 28,000 km/h.
That is why rockets lean over soon after launch and spend most of their effort gaining sideways speed rather than height.
Launching eastwards also borrows a boost from Earth's own rotation.
Pioneers to reusable rockets.
The Chinese used gunpowder rockets in war by the 1200s.
Around 1903 the Russian schoolteacher Konstantin Tsiolkovsky published the equation linking a rocket's speed to its exhaust speed and fuel load.
In 1926 American physicist Robert Goddard launched the first liquid-fuelled rocket in Massachusetts; it flew for about two and a half seconds.
Germany's V-2 of World War II, the first large guided ballistic missile, later helped both the US and Soviet space programs.
For most of the space age, rockets were thrown away after one use, like building a new airliner for every flight.
The Space Shuttle, 1981 to 2011, was partly reusable but slow and costly to refurbish.
In December 2015 SpaceX landed a Falcon 9 first stage upright, and it now routinely reflies boosters, some more than 30 times.
Rockets in Australia.
Australia has a real place in rocket history.
From 1947 the vast Woomera range in outback South Australia was used by Britain and Australia to test missiles and research rockets.
In November 1967 WRESAT, Australia's first satellite, was launched from Woomera on a modified American rocket, putting Australia among the first few nations with a satellite in orbit.
The Australian Space Agency was set up in 2018, and several Australian companies are developing launch vehicles and satellites.
Across the Tasman, Rocket Lab launches small satellites from New Zealand's Mahia Peninsula.
Next time you see a launch, you'll know it's Newton doing the work.
The key idea: Rockets work by Newton's third law: they throw gas backwards, so the rocket goes forwards, even in a vacuum.
Part two. The Space Race.
In 1957 a metal ball the size of a beach ball started beeping overhead, and two superpowers began racing to the Moon.
Cold War and Sputnik.
After World War II, the United States and the Soviet Union became rivals in the Cold War, a long standoff that stopped short of direct war.
Space became a stage for that contest.

Each side wanted to prove its system produced better science, and the stakes were military as well as symbolic: a rocket that could orbit a satellite could also carry a nuclear warhead across the world.
On 4 October 1957 the Soviet Union launched Sputnik 1, the first artificial satellite.
It was a polished metal sphere about 58 centimetres across, weighing roughly 84 kilograms.
It circled Earth every 96 minutes, simply transmitting a beeping radio signal.
The launch shocked Americans, who had assumed they were ahead.
A month later Sputnik 2 carried a dog named Laika, the first animal to orbit Earth; she did not survive.
Soviet firsts.
The Soviets kept claiming the headlines.
Luna 2 reached the Moon's surface in 1959.
On 12 April 1961, Yuri Gagarin, a 27-year-old air force pilot, became the first human in space aboard Vostok 1.
He orbited Earth once in about 108 minutes, then ejected during descent and parachuted down, as designed.
His cry of "Poyekhali", "Let's go", became famous.
He died in a jet training crash in 1968, aged 34.
In June 1963 Valentina Tereshkova became the first woman in space, spending almost three days in orbit.
On 18 March 1965 Alexei Leonov made the first spacewalk from Voskhod 2.
His suit ballooned so much that he had to let air out to squeeze back inside.
America responds.
The US answered quickly.
On 31 January 1958 it launched Explorer 1, whose instruments detected the Van Allen radiation belts, bands of charged particles trapped by Earth's magnetic field.
Later that year the government created NASA to run a civilian space program.
Sputnik also prompted major new US spending on science and maths education.
Alan Shepard became the first American in space on 5 May 1961, on a 15-minute suborbital hop.
In February 1962 John Glenn became the first American to orbit Earth, circling it three times.
As his capsule passed over Western Australia, the people of Perth switched on their lights, earning it the nickname "City of Light".
The Moon goal.
Stung by Gagarin's flight, President John F.
Kennedy told Congress in May 1961 that America should land a man on the Moon and return him safely before the decade was out.
In 1962 in Texas he added: "We choose to go to the Moon in this decade and do the other things, not because they are easy, but because they are hard."
The goal gave the race a clear finish line.
At its peak, Apollo employed roughly 400,000 people across government and industry.
Astronauts first had to master untried skills.
The US Gemini program, flying two-person crews in 1965 and 1966, practised spacewalks, flights of up to two weeks, and the first docking of two spacecraft in orbit.
Meanwhile the Soviet program lost its brilliant chief designer, Sergei Korolev, who died in 1966.
How it ended.
The race had real costs.
In January 1967 a fire during a ground test of Apollo 1 killed three astronauts, and months later cosmonaut Vladimir Komarov died when the parachute of Soyuz 1 failed.
The Soviets' giant N1 Moon rocket failed all four of its launch attempts.
In July 1969 Apollo 11 landed on the Moon, effectively settling the race.
By 1975 the mood had shifted.
In the Apollo-Soyuz mission, American and Soviet crews docked and shook hands in orbit.
That spirit later grew into the International Space Station.
The key idea: The Space Race grew from Cold War rivalry and missile technology, starting with Sputnik 1 in 1957.
Part three. Apollo and the Moon landing.
In July 1969 about 600 million people watched two men walk on the Moon, and those pictures reached the world through a dish in a sheep paddock in New South Wales.
One small step.
Apollo 11 launched from Florida on 16 July 1969 with Neil Armstrong, Buzz Aldrin and Michael Collins.
NASA used a plan called lunar orbit rendezvous.
Collins stayed in orbit in the command module, Columbia, while a light, spidery lander called Eagle carried the other two down to the Sea of Tranquillity.
That was 20 July in US time and 21 July in Australia.
The landing was tense.
Computer alarms flashed, and Armstrong steered past a boulder field by hand, with less than a minute of fuel to spare by some estimates.
Hours later he said, 'That's one small step for man, one giant leap for mankind.'
Aldrin followed about 20 minutes later.
The pair walked for roughly two and a half hours.
The Saturn V and beyond.
Getting there took the Saturn V, a three-stage rocket about 110 metres tall.
Its five first-stage engines burned roughly 13 tonnes of propellant every second.
It flew 13 times between 1967 and 1973 and never lost a crew.
Only the small command module came home; Apollo 11 splashed down in the Pacific on 24 July.
Apollo 12 landed in November 1969, beside an older robotic probe.
Apollo 13 never landed: an oxygen tank exploded, and the crew survived by using the lunar module as a lifeboat.
The last three landings carried a battery-powered buggy, the Lunar Roving Vehicle.
In all, six missions landed and 12 men walked on the Moon.
Apollo 17 left in December 1972, and no one has been back since.
The Parkes dish.
Because Earth was turning, the Moon was above Australia when Armstrong stepped out, so Australian stations did vital work.
The first TV images came through the Honeysuckle Creek tracking station near Canberra.
Minutes later, the CSIRO's 64-metre radio telescope at Parkes, in central-west New South Wales, took over and supplied the clearer pictures for most of the moonwalk.
Strong gusts of wind buffeted the dish, beyond its normal safe limits, but staff kept it tracking.
The story inspired the 2000 Australian film The Dish.
Rocks, quakes and proof.
The six landings brought back about 382 kilograms of lunar rock and soil, still studied by scientists around the world, including in Australia.
In 2022 scientists opened an Apollo 17 sample that had stayed vacuum-sealed since 1972.
Seismometers showed the Moon has moonquakes.
When Apollo 12 crashed its discarded lander stage into the surface, the Moon rang for nearly an hour, like a bell, because the dry, cold rock barely dampens vibrations.
Conspiracy theories say the landings were faked.
Yet around 400,000 people worked on Apollo, and the Soviet Union, which tracked the missions and had every reason to expose a hoax, never disputed them.
The laser mirrors left behind still work, and NASA's Lunar Reconnaissance Orbiter has photographed the landing sites, even the astronauts' footpaths.
Back to the Moon.
After five decades, humans are going back.
NASA's Artemis program is named after Apollo's twin sister in Greek mythology.
Artemis I flew uncrewed around the Moon in late 2022.
In April 2026, Artemis II sent four astronauts, including a Canadian, around the Moon and back without landing.
Later missions aim to land astronauts near the lunar south pole.
Permanently shadowed craters there may hold water ice that could supply drinking water, oxygen and even rocket fuel.
China has also announced plans to land astronauts by 2030.
When you look at the Moon, you're looking at a place humans have walked.
The key idea: Apollo 11 put Neil Armstrong and Buzz Aldrin on the Moon on 20 July 1969, US time, using a small lander, while Michael Collins stayed in orbit.
Part four. Australia's place in space.
A sheep paddock dish carried Apollo 11's moonwalk to the world, and a quiet desert range launched a satellite in 1967.
Australia's space story is bigger than most people know.
Woomera and WRESAT.
In 1947, Britain and Australia agreed to build a long-range weapons testing site in the South Australian outback.
The town of Woomera, named after an Aboriginal spear-thrower, grew up to support it.
The range stretched well over a thousand kilometres across the desert, giving room to fire rockets far from populated areas.
In the mid-1960s the United States offered Australia a spare Redstone rocket.
Scientists in Salisbury, South Australia, built a small satellite, WRESAT, in under a year.
It launched from Woomera on 29 November 1967, making Australia one of the first handful of nations to launch a satellite from its own territory.
It measured the Sun's radiation and the upper atmosphere before burning up in January 1968.
Britain's only satellite on a British rocket, Prospero, followed from Woomera in 1971.
The Dish at Parkes.
The Parkes radio telescope opened in 1961 among the sheep paddocks of central western New South Wales, its 64-metre dish among the most advanced in the world.
In July 1969, when Neil Armstrong stepped onto the Moon, it was high over Australia.
The first minutes of television were received by NASA's Honeysuckle Creek station near Canberra, which captured Armstrong climbing down the ladder.
Parkes then took over and supplied the pictures for most of the roughly two-and-a-half-hour moonwalk, despite strong winds that pushed the dish close to its safety limits.
The 2000 film The Dish dramatised the story, with some liberties.
In 2020 the telescope also received the Wiradjuri name Murriyang.
Listening to the deep.

To keep in touch with distant spacecraft as Earth rotates, NASA built three tracking stations roughly a third of the way around the globe from one another: Goldstone in California, Madrid in Spain, and Tidbinbilla near Canberra.
At any moment at least one can see a given spacecraft.

The Canberra Deep Space Communication Complex, run on NASA's behalf by Australia's national science agency CSIRO, has helped communicate with missions such as Voyager, the Mars rovers and New Horizons.
Parkes has made discoveries of its own.
In 2007, astronomers searching its archived data found the first known fast radio burst, a millisecond flash of radio waves from far beyond our galaxy, opening up an entirely new field of astronomy.
The Skylab fine.
Skylab, America's first space station, re-entered the atmosphere in July 1979, earlier than planned, and broke up over the Indian Ocean and southern Western Australia.
Debris rained down around the town of Esperance and across the Nullarbor, though no one was hurt.
The Shire of Esperance issued NASA a light-hearted 400-dollar fine for littering.
A San Francisco newspaper offered 10,000 dollars for the first piece of Skylab delivered to its office.
It was claimed by a 17-year-old from Esperance, Stan Thornton, who flew to the United States with fragments.
The fine went unpaid for 30 years, until a Californian radio host raised the money from listeners and paid it in 2009.
Australians in orbit.
Paul Scully-Power, an Australian-born oceanographer, flew aboard the Space Shuttle Challenger in 1984 as a payload specialist.
Adelaide-born engineer Andy Thomas became a NASA astronaut and flew four missions, including a long stay on the Russian space station Mir in 1998.
In 2024 Katherine Bennell-Pegg became the first astronaut to graduate from training under the Australian flag, completing the European Space Agency's basic astronaut training.
Australia established its own Australian Space Agency in 2018.
Its deserts remain useful too.
In 2010 and 2020, Japanese Hayabusa capsules carrying samples from asteroids parachuted down near Woomera, bringing pieces of other worlds to Australian soil.
The remote outback that suited rocket tests also suits recovering spacecraft.
The key idea: Woomera, a remote rocket range in South Australia, launched Australia's first satellite, WRESAT, in 1967.
Quick recall. Answer out loud, or just in your head.
Question one. Why can a rocket work in the vacuum of space?
Answer. It pushes gas backwards and is pushed forwards.
Question two. Why did Sputnik alarm Americans beyond its beeping signal?
Answer. The same rockets could carry warheads.
Question three. What was the 'lunar orbit rendezvous' plan used for Apollo 11?
Answer. One astronaut stayed in orbit as a lander took two down.
Question four. Why was Woomera chosen as a rocket range?
Answer. It was remote, with room to fire rockets.
That's the end of this episode. The questions are waiting in your review, so you can lock in what you heard.
